text: In a circular orbit, gravity is the only central force acting on the satellite, so GMm/r² = mv²/r, from which v = √(GM/r) follows. Hence the orbital speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the radius: a satellite moving slowly in a circular orbit must be farther from Earth. Therefore, if the satellite’s speed decreases while it remains in a circular orbit, its orbital radius increases. Its orbital period, T = 2πr/v, also increases, because the path becomes longer while the speed decreases; this agrees with Kepler’s third law, T² ∝ r³.
